opus-5.5.text:
I didn't have a grand master plan at the beginning. Looking back, though, each internship ended up giving me something different, and over time I became more deliberate about what I was looking for.

Early in my PhD, the main goal was simply exposure. I wanted to see how research worked outside my own lab. How do people in industry labs pick problems? How fast do they move? What does a strong researcher's daily workflow actually look like? You can read papers forever, but sitting next to people who are doing it and watching how they debug, argue, and decide what's worth pursuing teaches you a different kind of knowledge.

Later it became more about the people. I came to believe that the most valuable thing in an internship isn't the paper, though of course the paper matters. It's the chance to work closely with someone whose taste you admire. When I had the opportunity to work with researchers like Kaiming, what I really wanted to absorb was how they think. How simple can you make an idea? How do you know when an experiment is telling you something real? When should you stop adding complexity and strip things back? That sense of research taste is very hard to learn from a distance.

I also tried to treat internships as a way to step slightly outside my comfort zone. I'd pick something adjacent to my thesis work but not identical to it, so I'd come back with a new tool or a new perspective rather than just more of the same. Sometimes that worked well and sometimes less so, but even the less successful ones helped me figure out what I didn't want to do, which is also useful.

And honestly, part of it was practical too. Industry labs had compute and scale that a university lab often couldn't match, especially as deep learning took off. So some questions you could only really explore there.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say I went from "let me see what's out there" to "let me find the right people and the right problem, and learn how they think." The second mindset turned out to matter much more in the long run.

r001.rationale: He says each internship gave him something different and that he became more deliberate about what he sought, describing distinct aims such as exposure, learning from specific researchers, and exploring adjacent topics.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't have a grand plan at the start. When I was a PhD student at UC San Diego with Zhuowen Tu, I just knew I wanted to see how research worked outside of a university lab, because the academic setting can be a bit isolated. You're working on your own problem, with your own advisor, and you don't really know how the rest of the field thinks.

So my first internships were more about exposure. I wanted to be in a room with people who were doing things I didn't know how to do, and to see what problems they considered important. At a place like Google or Adobe, the scale of the data and the engineering culture were just different from what I had in school, and that changed my taste for what a good problem looks like. I started to care more about whether an idea would still hold up when you scale it, rather than whether it beat a benchmark by half a point.

Later on, the internship at Facebook AI Research was very different, because by then I had a clearer sense of what I wanted. I had done the ResNeXt work there, and I wanted to be around people like Kaiming and Ross, who had a very particular way of doing research. Very simple ideas, very carefully executed, and a lot of discipline about what to include and what to leave out. That was something I really wanted to learn, and it's hard to learn from papers. You have to watch how people make decisions day to day, what they reject, which experiments they don't bother running.

So if I had to summarize it, early internships were for figuring out what the field cared about, and later ones were for learning how specific people I admired actually worked. The second one turned out to matter much more for me than the first.

r001.rationale: The response describes distinct aims across the internships: early ones provided exposure to industry research and its priorities, while a later one was intended to teach him how specific researchers worked.

astra-6.text:
I think I approached each internship as a chance to try a different research environment. It wasn’t just about the particular project. I wanted to understand how people chose problems, how they collaborated, and how much freedom I would have to explore an idea.

And what I wanted changed as I got more experience. Early on, you need guidance—you want to work with someone you can learn from. Later, you start to have your own questions, and you want an environment where you can pursue them and get good feedback. So for me, internships were also a way to learn what kind of researcher I wanted to become, and what kind of environment would help me get there.

r001.rationale: He says he approached each internship as a chance to try a different research environment, clearly conveying that he deliberately sought a different experience at each one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what I wanted changed over time. Early on, I wanted exposure—to see how people in different groups approached research, how they picked problems, and what the day-to-day process looked like. You don’t really get that from reading their papers.

Later, I became more interested in finding an environment that complemented what I was getting in my PhD. An internship is a chance to work with people who have different intuitions, different resources, and different ways of deciding what matters. I wanted to learn from that, rather than just go somewhere and continue exactly the same project.

Of course, you hope to produce a good paper. But I think the longer-term value is developing your own taste: learning which questions excite you, what kind of collaboration works for you, and what kind of researcher you want to become.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing goals over time and valuing different research environments, but does not clearly state that he deliberately sought a different experience at each internship.
